candidateRows: Broad naturalism should accept the explanatory resources of physical, biological, and human sciences according to the phenomena being investigated.
This defines Clayton's pluralistic alternative to narrower naturalism and establishes the initial framework for the debate over explanatory adequacy.
After proposing a collegial discussion rather than a formal debate, Clayton opens the substantive exchange by defining his preferred form of naturalism.
An evolutionary account of human minds, morality, art, and humor can give cultural evolution a major role rather than reducing the explanation to genes.
The move rejects the suggestion that Dennett's naturalism excludes higher-level human sciences by incorporating cultural evolution into the naturalistic account.
Clayton's suggestion that his broad explanatory naturalism clashes with Dennett's narrower form of naturalism.
Clayton has just described a broad naturalism spanning several sciences and invited Dennett to identify where their approaches actually conflict.
Physical law constrains every action, while design-level and intentional-level descriptions remain practically indispensable ways of explaining organized systems and agents.
This supplies Dennett's core account of how physical determination coexists with autonomous higher-level explanation, directly addressing the debate's explanatory scope.
Clayton's claim that Dennett is reluctant to move from physical explanation to explanations involving persons and intentions.
Clayton interprets Dennett's physical, design, and intentional stances as showing excessive caution about personal and intentional explanations.
Intentional explanations should be treated as genuinely causal and realistic in the natural world, not merely as useful ways of treating physical systems.
The move isolates a foundational disagreement over whether mental and intentional descriptions identify real causes or only predictive interpretive perspectives.
Dennett's explanation of the intentional stance as treating a system like a roughly rational agent for predictive purposes.
Dennett has explained the hierarchy from physical description through design description to intentional prediction using a chess-playing computer.
Intentional states can furnish robust causal explanations because some regularities cannot be understood without characterizing what an agent realizes, decides, or represents.
This directly answers the charge of instrumentalism and asserts that intentional-level causation is genuine even though physical and biological causation also operate.
Clayton's contention that Dennett withdraws causal realism when explanation reaches the intentional stance.
Clayton has distinguished their shared realism about physical and biological causation from what he sees as Dennett's weaker attitude toward mental causes.
Intentional patterns are real features of the world even though their kind of realism differs from stronger theories that reify mental entities.
The distinction between real patterns and more inflationary realism is essential to Dennett's naturalistic account of mind and answers the recurring ontological criticism.
Clayton's renewed suggestion that Dennett becomes hesitant when moving from useful intentional explanations to what is really in the world.
After Dennett gives causal examples, Clayton argues that their practical usefulness may not establish full ontological realism about the mental level.
The intentional stance depends on roughly rational organization and can cease to apply when that organization fails, while physical causation continues without interruption.
The failure-condition argument explains the asymmetrical dependence among explanatory stances and clarifies what Dennett means by physical hegemony without eliminating mental explanation.
Clayton's inference that accepting multiple explanatory levels removes any meaningful priority among physical, design, and intentional accounts.
Clayton continues to connect Dennett's references to physical hegemony with an alleged reluctance to grant equal ontological standing to higher-level causes.
A properly organized physical system is sufficient for mentality; no additional mental substance is required beyond the successful functional organization of its physical components.
This is the clearest naturalistic sufficiency claim in the exchange and directly rejects an ontologically additional ingredient in the explanation of mind.
Clayton's claim that Dennett silently stops granting full causal and ontological reality once explanation moves beyond neurology.
Following the black-box example, Clayton argues that Dennett accepts physical organization but exits the hierarchy before granting independent reality to higher mental levels.
The philosophical term for subjective experiential properties is too theoretically unsettled to support reliable argument, as disagreement revealed by change-blindness cases demonstrates.
The move challenges a principal conceptual basis for treating subjective experience as an irreducible addition to naturalistic accounts of mind and agency.
Clayton's allegation that Dennett resists ontological commitment precisely when the discussion turns to subjects, subjective states, and qualia.
Clayton argues that Dennett accepts folk-psychological description but retreats from realism about subjective states, prompting a focused exchange about qualia.
Personhood centrally consists in real subjective and internal states that arise from brain processes yet remain indispensable parts of agency and self-understanding.
The claim connects the technical dispute about consciousness to the debate's broader account of persons, preserving subjective experience as explanatorily and ontologically central.
Dennett's treatment of disagreement about qualia as largely a problem of unstable philosophical terminology rather than a deeper ontological divide.
The moderator asks how the realism dispute bears on larger questions, including views about God, after Dennett's extended critique of qualia terminology.

Religious communities bear special responsibility for confronting extremists within their own traditions, while benign religious activity can unintentionally provide reputational cover for malignant forms.
The argument directly contests whether benign religion can be separated from harmful religion and identifies an institutional mechanism by which the former may shelter the latter.
Clayton's proposal to distinguish and encourage benign religious communities instead of treating all religion alike.

After Clayton advocates dialogue with socially constructive religious positions, Dennett argues that every tradition contains fanaticism and that adherents must actively confront their own extremists.
Progressive religious communities actively oppose fanaticism, violence, irrationalism, and fundamentalism while making commitment to reason central to their religious practice.
This rebuttal challenges Dennett's institutional-cover argument by asserting that reason-guided religious groups actively criticize abuses committed under religious authority.
Dennett's claim that liberal believers fail to identify and condemn radical members of their own religious traditions.

Dennett contrasts scientific self-correction with an alleged failure by liberal Christians to condemn fundamentalists; Clayton answers with counterexamples and a reason-centered model of progressive religion.
A mature religious stance integrates altruistic community, reflective philosophical inquiry, and a metaphysical account in which experienced reality may participate in a deeper or personal ground.
The move supplies the debate's principal affirmative account of what religion adds beyond naturalistic description: an integrated moral, intellectual, and metaphysical framework.
Following discussion of religion's social benefits, Clayton explains when religious explanation becomes substantive and outlines several discussable hypotheses about a deeper source of reality.
A purported transcendent reality cannot be distinguished from the naturalist's reality if its nature is declared mysterious or unknowable, leaving the theist unable to establish a genuine difference.
This is a core naturalist objection to religious ultimacy: an unknowable transcendent posit lacks enough determinate content to contrast meaningfully with naturalism.
Clayton's claim that his open, nonauthoritarian theistic worldview remains genuinely different from Dennett's non-theistic worldview.
Clayton has defended a theism that remains open to discussion and avoids scriptural trump cards; Dennett presses whether an admittedly mysterious transcendence can mark any knowable disagreement.
Morality requires no divine command because its strongest available ground is a revisable secular community of mutually persuading participants in which no revelation receives automatic authority.
The move squarely addresses the motion's morality component by rejecting divine-command grounding and offering a naturalistic, public, corrigible basis for ethical judgment.

After agreement about philosophy as inquiry into unresolved questions, Dennett turns to morality, invokes the divine-command dilemma, and proposes inclusive mutual persuasion as its secular foundation.
Religion is not required for morality, but moral life belongs within a wider worldview whose distinctive religious component includes substantive beliefs about ultimate reality.
The argument concedes secular moral possibility while preserving religion's claimed explanatory addition through the integration of ethics, interpretation, and beliefs about ultimacy.
Dennett's contention that Clayton's reasonable moral and philosophical outlook appears entirely secular and lacks a supernatural distinction.
Asked what a description of him as thoroughly secular would omit, Clayton identifies worldview and ultimate-reality beliefs as the element not captured by shared altruism and inquiry alone.
Ultimate reality is exhausted by the universe and its laws, with no apparent room or explanatory need for anything beyond nature; theology arises from attempts to preserve inherited religion.
This move gives the naturalist position on ultimacy and explains religious metaphysics genealogically rather than treating it as an additional explanatory level of reality.
Clayton's assertion that a religious person holds distinctive substantive beliefs about an ultimate reality beyond behavioral manifestations.

After Clayton says religion includes beliefs about ultimacy, Dennett identifies nature itself as ultimate and portrays theology as the intellectual reshaping of inherited doctrines into assertable forms.

Theism and naturalism express a genuine worldview disagreement because the theist regards the universe as contained within a broader and deeper ultimate reality, a claim open to civil philosophical argument.
The move states the religious alternative to naturalistic ultimacy in its clearest form and argues that the disagreement can be reasoned about without appeal to scriptural authority.
Dennett's claim that nature leaves no room for anything beyond it and that theologians merely rehabilitate inherited religious views.
Clayton rejects the negative genealogy of theology, isolates the disagreement over what is ultimate, and maintains that theistic metaphysics can remain part of ordinary civil philosophical debate.
A claim about ultimate reality lacks intelligible epistemic content unless its proponent can identify some possible experience that would reveal the claim to be mistaken.
The challenge tests whether the religious framework is answerable to experience and therefore whether it functions as a substantive explanatory claim rather than an insulated interpretation.
Clayton's account of religious worldview claims as coherent, discussable positions with practical and conceptual entailments.
Clayton has described worldviews as integrated interpretations whose entailments can be compared; Dennett responds by demanding a recognizable condition under which the theistic view could fail.
Religious beliefs about ultimate reality can change in response to experience, including suffering, and such changes alter what a person believes exists rather than merely changing behavior.
The response addresses the epistemic-content objection by identifying experience-sensitive revision and insisting that theism and naturalism make genuinely different ontological commitments.
Dennett's demand for a possible experience that could make Clayton judge his belief about ultimate reality to be wrong.
In response to the falsifiability challenge, Clayton cites reactions to tragic death and religious conversion, then emphasizes that these shifts concern what ultimately exists in the world.
